questions.q: Name the five major physical locations Gandhi visits between meeting Rajkumar Shukla in Lucknow and beginning his inquiry in Champaran.
questions.a: The five major locations are: (1) Lucknow (Congress session), (2) Cawnpore (appointment), (3) Ahmedabad (ashram), (4) Calcutta (meeting point with Shukla), (5) Patna (Rajendra Prasad's house), then (6) Muzzafarpur (Kripalani/Malkani), and finally (7) Motihari/Champaran. A student who lists only "Bihar" or "Champaran" misses the deliberate journey structure that builds narrative tension and shows Gandhi's methodical fact-finding.

questions.q: Explain why the author describes the servants at Rajendra Prasad's house not allowing Gandhi to draw water from the well. What atmosphere does this detail create?
questions.a: This detail reveals the entrenched caste hierarchy and untouchability practices that even Gandhi's allies unconsciously upheld. It creates an atmosphere of deep-rooted social injustice that parallels the economic exploitation by British planters. A student who says "it shows Gandhi was poor" or "it shows servants were rude" misses the systemic critique — the detail establishes that the fight in Champaran is against layered oppression, not just landlords.

questions.q: In the Muzzafarpur section, Fischer writes: "In smaller localities, the Indians were afraid to show sympathy for advocates of home-rule." Apply this observation to explain the atmosphere when Gandhi stays at Professor Malkani's house.
questions.a: Professor Malkani, a government school teacher, harboring Gandhi — a known home-rule advocate — is an act of quiet defiance. The atmosphere here is tense but hopeful: Malkani risks his career, showing that Gandhi's presence inspires courage even in the fearful. A student who only notes "Gandhi stayed safely" misses the subversive atmosphere; the detail "extraordinary thing in those days" signals that ordinary Indians are beginning to overcome fear, foreshadowing the mass demonstration at Motihari.

questions.q: Compare the atmosphere at the Motihari courthouse before Gandhi's trial with the atmosphere in the Champaran villages after the settlement. What specific sensory details mark the shift?
questions.a: Before the trial: "Motihari black with peasants," "spontaneous demonstration," "dreaded and unquestioned" British might — atmosphere of tense confrontation, collective fear turning into mass courage. After settlement: "primary schools opened in six villages," "castor oil, quinine, sulphur ointment," "filthy state of women's clothes" — atmosphere of constructive, patient nation-building. The shift is from dramatic public resistance to quiet, daily empowerment. A student who describes both as "happy" or "peaceful" fails to distinguish revolutionary tension from constructive hope.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to describe the indigo sharecropping system through the physical landscape ("large estates owned by Englishmen," "chief commercial crop was indigo") rather than only through peasant testimony. How does this shape the reader's understanding of the atmosphere of exploitation?
questions.a: By grounding exploitation in the land itself — "most of the arable land... divided into large estates" — Fischer makes the oppression structural and inescapable, not just interpersonal. The atmosphere becomes one of systemic entrapment: the soil, the crop, the contract (15% indigo) all bind the peasant. A student who prefers "peasant voices only" misses how the impersonal geographic/economic description creates a heavier, more pervasive atmosphere of injustice that requires Gandhi's structural solution (commission, settlement, schools).

questions.q: Write a 100-word descriptive paragraph from the perspective of a sharecropper waiting outside the Motihari courthouse on the morning of Gandhi's trial, using at least three sensory details from the text to convey the atmosphere.
questions.a: A strong answer will include: visual ("black with peasants," "vast multitude"), auditory ("vehement protests of landlords" earlier, or the silence of the crowd), tactile/olfactory (dust, heat, sweat), and emotional shift from fear to "liberation from fear." It should show the crowd as active participants ("helped them regulate the crowd"), not passive spectators. A weak answer uses generic "crowd" and "nervous" without textual anchors.
